title: Health and the doctor
cando: say what is wrong, make an appointment and read a medicine label

about.text: In this lesson you are ill and you need help. You say what is wrong at a chemist, you phone a clinic to make an appointment, and you read a medicine label so you know how much to take.
goals: Say what is wrong: I've got a headache. My back hurts. I feel ill.
Understand advice with should: You should rest.
Read a medicine label: how much, how often, and what not to do.
Write a short note to take to the doctor.
Make an appointment on the phone.

chapters.title: At the chemist
chapters.text:
In this lesson you are ill, and you need help.
First, you go to a chemist. A chemist sells medicine and gives advice. You do not need an appointment.
The chemist asks: What's the matter?
You say what is wrong.
At the end, people often say: I hope you feel better soon.

chapters.title: Three ways to say what is wrong
chapters.text:
There are three ways to say what is wrong.
One: I've got, and the problem. I've got a headache. I've got a cough.
Two: my, the part of your body, and hurts. My back hurts. My throat hurts.
Three: I feel, and how you feel. I feel ill. I feel tired.
To give advice, use should. You should rest. You should see a doctor.
Do not say should to. Say: you should rest.

chapters.title: A medicine label
chapters.text:
Next, you read a medicine label.
A label answers four questions. How much? How often? How much in one day? And what must you not do?
Read it slowly. The numbers are important.
Then you write a short note for the doctor: what is wrong, when it started, and one question.

chapters.title: Making an appointment
chapters.text:
Then you phone a clinic and make an appointment.
Say: I'd like to make an appointment, please.
The receptionist asks your name, your problem and a time.
Say the time back to check it: Four o'clock? Yes, that's fine.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a short story about a visit to the doctor.
Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

warmup.prompt: You feel ill. Where do you go first?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. For a small problem, many people go to a chemist first. It is quick, and you do not need an appointment.

conversation.title: At the chemist
conversation.setting: Ana does not feel well. She goes to the chemist near her home.
lines: Yes, please. I don't feel well.
I'm sorry to hear that. What's the matter?
I've got a sore throat, and my head hurts.
No, I haven't. But I feel very tired.
OK. Take these tablets. One tablet, three times a day, after food.
One tablet, three times a day, after food. Thank you.
You should rest and drink a lot of water. If you don't feel better in three days, see a doctor.
You're welcome. I hope you feel better soon.

questions.q: How often does Ana take the tablets?
questions.why: The chemist says: One tablet, three times a day, after food.

questions.q: When should Ana see a doctor?
questions.a: if she doesn't feel better in three days
questions.why: The chemist says: If you don't feel better in three days, see a doctor.

sound.title: hurt and heart
sound.explain: These two words sound different. Hurt has the sound in her and bird. Heart has the sound in car and park. Listen, then say each group.
lines: The doctor listened to my heart.

sayIt.instructions: Say Ana's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Is your voice clear?

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Each one says what is wrong in a different way. The last one gives advice.
spot.question: Which sentence names the problem? Which names a part of the body? Which says how Ana feels? Which gives advice?
spot.answer: I've got + the problem: a sore throat. My + a part of the body + hurts: my head hurts. I feel + how you are: very tired. You should + a verb gives advice: you should rest.

rules.title: Three ways to say what is wrong
rule: I've got + a problem: I've got a headache. I've got a cough.
My + part of the body + hurts: My back hurts. My feet hurt.
I feel + how you are: I feel ill. I feel tired.
Ask: What's the matter? Have you got a temperature?
rules.mistake: Not: My head is hurt. Say: My head hurts.

rules.title: Advice with should
rule: You should + a verb: You should rest. You should see a doctor.
Not: You should to rest. Not: She shoulds rest.
No: You shouldn't go to work today.
Question: Should I take it after food?
rules.mistake: Not: You should to drink water. Say: You should drink water.

Two feet, so hurt, with no s.

should + a verb, with no to.

practice.q: Have you got a ___ ? Your head is very hot.
practice.why: A high temperature: your body is very hot.

practice.q: What's the ___ ? I've got a cough.
practice.why: What's the matter? asks what is wrong.

yourTurn.prompt: Your friend says: “I've got a bad cough, and I feel very tired.” Give your friend three pieces of advice. Use should and shouldn't.
yourTurn.model: You should rest. You should drink hot water with honey. You shouldn't go to work today. I hope you feel better soon.

text.title: A medicine label
text.body:
PRACTICE LABEL: this medicine does not exist

PARALEX 500 mg tablets
For headache, toothache and other pain
24 tablets

HOW MUCH AND HOW OFTEN
Adults and children over 12:
1 or 2 tablets every 4 to 6 hours.
Do not take more than 8 tablets in 24 hours.
Not for children under 12.

HOW TO TAKE
Take with water, after food.

WARNINGS
Do not take for more than 3 days.
Then see a doctor.
Do not drink alcohol with this medicine.

Keep away from children.
Use by: 09/2027

gist.a: pain, like a headache or toothache
gist.why: The label says: For headache, toothache and other pain.
Adults and children over 12. Not for children under 12.

detail.q: How many tablets can you take at one time?
How often can you take them?
What is the most you can take in one day?
detail.why: Do not take more than 8 tablets in 24 hours.

detail.q: You still have a headache after 3 days. What should you do?
detail.why: Do not take for more than 3 days. Then see a doctor.

model.title: A note for the doctor
model.body:
What is wrong: My back hurts. I've got a pain in my lower back.
When it started: On Monday, at work.
Better or worse: It is worse in the morning. It is better when I rest.
My question: Is it serious?

write.task: Write a note to take to the doctor. It can be real or made up. Write four lines, like the model: what is wrong, when it started, what makes it better or worse, and one question.
checklist: I said what is wrong: I've got …, my … hurts, or I feel …
I said when it started: on Monday, two days ago …
I wrote one question, with a question mark.
Every sentence starts with a capital letter.

card.title: Make an appointment
card.situation: You've got a bad cough and a temperature. It started on Saturday. You want to see a doctor today or tomorrow.
card.goal: Phone the clinic. Give your name, say what is wrong, and agree a time.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher is the receptionist. Phone the clinic and make your appointment. Then change roles.
doIt.wehel: You are a receptionist at a doctor's clinic. I am ill and I want an appointment. Ask my name, my problem and when I can come. Offer me two times. Use simple English.

model.title: The call
lines: Good morning, Park Road Clinic. How can I help?
Hello. I'd like to make an appointment, please.
Can you spell your family name, please?
I've got a bad cough and a temperature.
The doctor can see you today at four o'clock. Is that OK?
Four o'clock? Yes, that's fine. Thank you.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the chemist conversation in pairs, then change the problem: a cough, a stomach ache, a sore tooth.
Day 2: advice circle. Each learner says a problem, and the others give advice with should and shouldn't.
Day 3: the phone call. You are the receptionist. Each learner makes an appointment; change the names and the times.
Day 4: talk about the book, answer questions, and let two learners read their notes for the doctor aloud.
